status: Finished. All three improvements are done. Peak, from 1950: the top tier is Fangio, Senna, Clark, Schumacher and Stewart, and the model can't separate them. The second tier is Graham Hill, Verstappen, Lauda, Rindt, Alonso, Mansell, Piquet and Ascari. Combined 50/50, from 1970: Schumacher is alone in tier 1 (70% chance of being first). Tier 2 is Verstappen, Alonso, Senna and Hamilton. On career, Schumacher, Alonso, Verstappen and Hamilton share tier 1. None of the stronger-car versions improved prediction, so the main model is unchanged. Removing a single teammate usually moves a driver less than 0.2 places, but drivers alone in a strong car move more: Hamilton without Rosberg, Mansell without Patrese and Hill without Ginther. From 2018 the results-only model agrees with a lap-time model at 0.9 on season scores and on the order of the peak ranking.
note_peak: Some placings deserve suspicion before anyone reads them as findings. Frentzen and Kubica rank high, while Hamilton's peak is 2010–12 rather than a title run. In this 1970+ view Stewart's peak uses only his last three seasons, moves by about 0.6 depending on the warm-up, and leaves the top five with no warm-up at all. The all-time section below covers his earlier years. Each could be real or could come from who their teammates were. The 2018+ models also use different years and evidence, so their scores aren't directly comparable with the 1970+ ones.
note_adapt: Treat this as weak evidence. In tests with known answers, the 1970+ model only partly recovers the true order (0.56 for teams and 0.41 for rules on the final version). The convergence check is also weakest for the spread of the rules effect (R-hat 1.03). Schumacher's comeback seasons score far below his peak, but the model can't fully separate age, three years out and the 2010 car rules. So this doesn't prove he adapted badly, as you pointed out.
wet_text: Using your rule, a race counts as wet if at least 50% was run on inters or wets, changeable at 20–50%, and dry below that. From 2018 this uses real tyre data, giving 9 wet and 7 changeable races. For 1971–2017 there's no tyre data, so I estimated 116 races from reports, giving 44 wet and 35 changeable. On six 2018+ races that estimate was within 7 points of the truth. In the final known-answer test the 1970+ model recovers wet race pace at 0.42, wet qualifying at 0.30 and changeable pace at 0.33. So these scores show direction but shouldn't be used to separate individual drivers.
note_2012: Alonso's gain is the largest in this group, in a car ranked only 3rd. But his range overlaps Hamilton's and Vettel's, and a large part of the evidence is one teammate, Massa, whose own level is an estimate. It supports your view of that season without proving it. Vettel's gain is also limited by the ceiling, since he had the best car.
changes: Each driver gets their own penalty after changing team or rules, fading over about 6 races, measured against the typical driver.
50%+ on wet tyres is wet, 20–50% is changeable with its own score, the rest is dry. Tyre data from 2018, checked race reports before.
